message.content:
A CPU (Central Processing Unit) and a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) are both processors, but they’re designed for different workloads:

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| **Primary purpose** | General‑purpose computing – handles everything from OS tasks to application logic. | Parallel graphics rendering – originally for rasterizing images, now also used for parallel data processing. |
| **Core count** | Few cores (2–32 on consumer CPUs). | Hundreds or thousands of smaller cores. |
| **Core design** | Complex, high‑performance cores with deep pipelines, branch prediction, large caches, and sophisticated control logic. | Simpler, more uniform cores optimized for throughput; each core does less work individually but many can run simultaneously. |
| **Execution style** | Serial or low‑parallelism tasks; excels at branching and unpredictable code paths. | SIMD/SIMT style – same instruction executed across many data elements; great for data‑parallel workloads. |
| **Memory hierarchy** | Large L1/L2/L3 caches per core, fast access to main memory. | Smaller per‑core caches; relies heavily on high‑bandwidth memory (e.g., GDDR5/6). |
| **Typical workloads** | Operating system, single‑threaded applications, database queries, web servers. | Rendering graphics, machine learning inference/training, scientific simulations, cryptocurrency mining. |
| **Programming model** | Traditional imperative programming (C/C++, Java, etc.). | Parallel programming models like CUDA, OpenCL, Vulkan compute shaders, or higher‑level frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch). |

In short, a CPU is a versatile “master” processor good at handling diverse, sequential tasks, while a GPU is a specialized “worker” that shines when you need to perform the same operation on many pieces of data at once.
